name: L bracket
use: Back plate on the flat, shelf on top, gusset underneath: the part to bolt on when something has to stick out sideways and stay level.

name: Rod socket
use: Stands a round tube up off a cell face, so a mast, a stake or a conduit riser is carried by the cluster.

name: Leveling foot
use: Puts a captive nut on a face so a bought leveling bolt can take the weight, which is how a cluster gets level on ground that is not.

name: Ground anchor
use: Pins a cell to the ground through a hole sized for a stake or a heavy screw, for a build that has to stay where you put it.

name: Hook plate
use: Each plate carries two hooks side by side, so you bolt on as many as you want where you want them rather than committing a whole face to a rail.

name: Story splice
use: Ties two stacked cells across the joint line, the one accessory that reaches past its own story.

name: Keyhole hanger
use: Hangs a cell on screws that are already in a wall, so mounting is a lift and a drop rather than a drilling job through the cluster.

name: Cable comb
use: A block of teeth a cable pushes in between sideways, so a bundle is kept in order without anything to thread or undo.

name: Grab handle
use: A bar standing off the flat with room for a hand behind it, for a cell or a column that gets moved by its side rather than its top.

name: Pipe saddle, 3/4 in
use: A cradle that carries a run of rigid pipe against a cell, sized by nominal pipe size and closed with a cable tie, so the pipe is held by the cluster instead of resting on it.

name: Pipe saddle, 1/2 in
use: A cradle that carries a run of rigid pipe against a cell, sized by nominal pipe size and closed with a cable tie, so the pipe is held by the cluster instead of resting on it.

name: Pipe saddle, 1 in
use: A cradle that carries a run of rigid pipe against a cell, sized by nominal pipe size and closed with a cable tie, so the pipe is held by the cluster instead of resting on it.

name: Cascade pocket
use: A pocket that bolts to a cell's side flat and hangs one story down, so what it holds sits in front of the cell below. Its back plate covers that lower cell's bolt rectangle and side bore, so the flat it hangs over takes nothing else.

name: French cleat
use: Hangs a cell on a beveled strip screwed to the wall. The hook drops in behind the bevel and the cell's weight pulls it against the wall. The hook sits between the bolt columns, which leaves a driver room to reach every bolt head.

name: Cable comb, two stories tall
use: A block of teeth a cable pushes in between sideways, so a bundle is kept in order without anything to thread or undo.

name: French cleat, three stories tall
use: Hangs a cell on a beveled strip screwed to the wall. The hook drops in behind the bevel and the cell's weight pulls it against the wall. The hook sits between the bolt columns, which leaves a driver room to reach every bolt head.

name: Keyhole hanger, two stories tall
use: Hangs a cell on screws that are already in a wall, so mounting is a lift and a drop rather than a drilling job through the cluster.

name: Keyhole hanger, three stories tall
use: Hangs a cell on screws that are already in a wall, so mounting is a lift and a drop rather than a drilling job through the cluster.

name: Cascade pocket, three stories tall
use: A pocket that bolts to a cell's side flat and hangs one story down, so what it holds sits in front of the cell below. Its back plate covers that lower cell's bolt rectangle and side bore, so the flat it hangs over takes nothing else.

name: Pipe socket
use: Bolts a glue-in socket for 3/4 in pipe to any face that takes a bolt-on: a side flat, or the lid of a bolt cover. Solvent-weld a pipe into it with PVC primer and cement and the cell becomes a joint in a structural PVC frame, with the pipe leaving straight out of the face.

name: Port plug
use: Blanks a side port you are not using, so a cell that is closed up looks finished and nothing gets in through a hole you left open.

name: Port louvre
use: Vents a closed cell without letting rain in, so a box that has to breathe can still stand outside.

name: Port screen
use: Passes air and keeps insects and debris out, so a cell can breathe through an opening that is still covered.

name: Port hose barb
use: Lands a hose on a cell, so water arrives and leaves through a spigot drawn for it rather than over an edge.

name: Port cable plate
use: Leads cable through a side port on finished holes, so wiring enters a closed cell through something drawn for it and each run has its own way in.

name: Side connector, single
use: Bridges the seam between two neighbouring cells and resists shear across it, for a cluster that gets pushed sideways rather than only loaded down.

name: Side connector, double
use: Bridges the seam between two neighbouring cells and resists shear across it, for a cluster that gets pushed sideways rather than only loaded down.

name: Blank plug
use: Fills an insert recess you are not using, so the face reads flat and the pocket stays clean.

name: Female socket
use: Seats in a recess and takes a stud, which makes it the bottom of every stacked insert.

name: Male stud
use: Threads through a seated socket and stands proud of the face, so it can carry whatever mounts above it.

name: Foot
use: Snaps onto a stud to give the face something to stand on, so a cell can rest on its cover rather than on its rim.

name: Zip-tie anchor
use: Seats in a recess and gives a cable tie something to pass through, so a bundle is anchored to the face instead of looped around it.

name: Trinity handle
use: Reaches across a whole triangle of studs, so a lift is shared between recesses instead of hanging off one, and the cell can be carried loaded.

name: Notch tray, male-female hand
use: Fills the empty position between two cells that stand side by side, bolted to both of them: a dovetail and four M6 on each of the two flats it meets. It is full height against the two cells and slopes away to a low rim at the open side, so it is a tray you reach into from the front of the notch. The two flats around a notch are always one of each gender, so it comes as a mirrored pair, and the notch decides which one fits.
